#3847. Former Dishonored designer joins the team on New Blood's Victorian immersive sim Gloomwood, with a new level and new weapons coming this year

Gloomwood, the Victorian survival horror immersive sim (or, wait, I'm getting reports that we shouldn't call it an immersive sim, apparently) by Dillon Rogers is a game that is quite happily inspired by its predecessors such as Thief, Resident Evil and Dishonored; you could call it 'Thief with guns', if you really wanted to. (Sorry, I've just seen that the domain for Gloomwood's site used to be 'residenthievil.com'. Wonderful). Now, that last inspiration has come full circle, as publisher New Blood Interactive's latest update post confirms that the newest member of the team is none other than former Dishonored designer Julien Eveillé.

In addition to his work at Arkane on Dishonored and its sequel, Deathloop, and even Marvel's Blade, Eveillé also developed his own indie horror, 2024's short and sweet Threshold. It's quite a legacy to add to this team, and his hiring is described by New Blood as an example of how "finding level designers who are up to the task of working on Gloomwood is not easy". The post also mentions that Eveillé will be added alongside "our new devs", implying that he's not the only new addition to the team.

Other than these new hires, the update is set to include quite a bit to change up Gloomwood and make it bigger. The highlight is the First National Bank level, which is described as "our largest and most intricately designed level yet", with the screenshots showing off a grand and imposing, yet claustrophobic in places, that makes the act of going to the bank even more intimidating than usual. The Bank is joined by the new stun prod weapon, which is self-explanatory, and the new Rat and Fishdog transformations, which let you sneak through crawlspaces and swim through dirtied waters respectively. That sneaking will be made more difficult by the addition of alarms and blood pools that both alert surrounding guards to your presence, though the new Crow King transformation offers a new, acid-belching way to take down any guards that come running.

The update is tentatively scheduled for "before the end of the year", but New Blood aren't setting down a specific release date. Rogers himself will also be going through back surgery very soon, for which I wish him a gentle recovery and, hopefully, as easy a return to work as possible.

#3846. 'I Mean, Guys, Really?!': GTA 7 Questions Batted Aside by Take-Two Boss

While it’s been available for several days now, I imagine you’re only just beginning to scratch the surface of GTA 6.

I’m now comfortably over 200 hours into my game, and it boggles my mind how much I’ve still got left to see. (I have been writing our GTA 6 guide simultaneously, though, so that is inflating my number a fair bit.)

I almost can’t believe business podcast TBPN is already asking Take-Two boss Strauss Zelnick about GTA 7, then – but it is.

The executive was fairly polite in his first response, saying:

“Once you get through several hundred hours of the most incredible fun you’ve ever heard, ask the question again.”

You’d have thought that would shut down the conversation, but no.

Zelnick was later pushed on how big the map in GTA 7 could be, and he launched a wry response:

“Let me check my watch. Oh, it’s still November 19th. And you’re asking a question about GTA 7. I mean, guys, really?”

The transcript makes Zelnick sound more agitated than he actually was, but I still find it crazy the hosts of TBPN thought it appropriate to mention the next game, when this one took 13 years to release.

Obviously the next step for Rockstar is the new version of GTA Online, but I think it’d be nice to reflect on what we have for a moment, before we start thinking about what’s to come.

Review GTA 6 (PS5) - The Greatest Open World Game Ever Made

Guide GTA 6 Guide: All Guides & Collectibles

As the Editor of Push Square, Sammy has over 15 years of experience analysing the world of PlayStation, from PS3 through PS5 and everything in between. He’s an expert on PS Studios and industry matters, as well as sports games and simulators. He also enjoys RPGs when he has the time to dedicate to them, and is a bit of a gacha whale.

Grand Theft Auto 6 is already enormously successful, having enjoyed "the biggest entertainment launch in history". But the current games industry is such that some Rockstar developers are still concerned about being laid off in the wake of its release. Writing for the Guardian prior to GTA 6's launch, Rockstar animation programmer Nestor Uriarte explained that although there is "no indication that layoffs are coming" it nonetheless "says a lot about the industry that even my colleagues and I, working on the biggest game of all time, are worried about getting laid off."

It might sound odd for the developers of such a hugely successful game to be worried about losing their jobs, but layoffs don't just occur when games or companies struggle commercially. A common cause of layoffs in the games industry is companies trying to reduce overheads after a game has launched, as the studio switches from full production to post-release support for their current game and planning for the next one.

It's partly why the industry seems to be in a constant, rolling state of layoffs, even when games appear to sell well. This issue was recently addressed by Jennifer Svedberg-Yen, the lead writer of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. Svedberg-Yen, who left Sandfall Interactive in July, claimed that the problem is exacerbated by an imbalance in who benefits financially when a game like Grand Theft Auto 6 launches.

"99 Metacritic score. Multiple award nominations before it even released. Massive sales and player engagement. Incredible amounts of tangible and intangible value creation. Yet the team is worried about layoffs," Svedberg-Yen wrote in an Instagram post. "So, who receives the lion's share of the profits from their labor? Not the vast majority of the creative team."

Svedberg-Yen pointed out that this is "one of the issues that happens when the people creating the value do not receive a proportionate amount of that value," adding that "In finance, we call that value extraction."

Svedberg-Yen also commented on the Rockstar team's ongoing efforts to unionise, with the team in the process of voting on whether or not it wants a union. If successful, the Rockstar Game Workers Union would become the biggest in the UK's gaming sector.

"I sincerely hope the Rockstar team is successful in unionizing," Svedberg-Yen wrote. "Layoffs during lulls in development cycles would work a lot better if teams were properly paid for the value they create, not just one-time, but throughout the life of the thing they created."

The games industry has seen a huge number of layoffs in the last few years. A recent report by GDC found that 34% of developers it surveyed had been laid off since 2024. Xbox alone has cut thousands of jobs, with more planned going into January 2027. Most recently, Firaxis, owned by GTA 6 publisher Take Two Interactive, reportedly laid off a third of its staff earlier this week as it works on a new XCOM.

#3844. You cannot replay missions in GTA 6, but you can use multiple save files, as Rockstar explains how it made missions "harder to fail"

You cannot replay GTA 6 missions again once you've completed them. This might be a shock to some people, since the option to do so was included in Rockstar games as recently as GTA 5, but here once you've made progress in the story, that's it. Our reviewer confirmed this in his 100+ hour playthrough of the title.

You can, of course, use the game's 15 save slots instead - but considering that there will be many, many more missions than there are slots, you're going to have to think about when and where you want to make a record of your progress. By my maths, that means you're going to want to make a new manual save for every 6.6 percent of the game you complete. There is, of course, an auto-save slot, too, that should help you out if you get Busted or Wasted. There will also be key story missions - you will be able to tell when they are, much like you could tell when there was about to be a big heist in GTA 5, a showdown in GTA: San Andreas, or a raid on a gang lord's mansion in GTA: Vice City - that you may want to save before attempting.

It seems, though, that it's going to be a bit harder than in previous games to hit that fail state in GTA 6. "The team embraced more of an open-ended design philosophy on this project," says David Hynd, vice president of technology on GTA 6. "For example, we really wanted to reduce the number of Mission fails for the player experimenting or trying something different. And we wanted to encourage the player to do what felt right to them for their particular play style."

That means that Rockstar, by considering its deployment of standard gameplay mechanics and enemy AI, and re-evaluating how it approached mission and level design, has created "many different ways" for you to approach any given mission in the game. The result? "It's a lot harder to keep Missions as open as possible (especially in a game as large as this), but the freedom and flexibility it allows the player was worth it," says Hynd. He also notes that the team expects players to "learn and reapply" consistent rules in terms of how the world works - and be surprised when they do and don't apply.

In the previous game, you could access any previous mission you'd completed and be able to play it again on a whim. For GTA 5, you'd simply boot up Story Mode, open the pause menu, go to Game > Replay Mission, and pick the mission you want to play. GTA 6's structure is more complicated, though, hence why Rockstar made the decision to make progress this linear.

GTA 6 comes out tomorrow. You can find a breakdown of all the global launch times for GTA 6 at the link, and read our 5-star review of the game here. If you want to, ahem, 'travel to New Zealand' to get ahead of the timezones, it seems the country would be happy to have you.

A year ago, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 swept through many an awards show and broke a few records along the way. It was a performance so massive that actor Rich Keeble still can't "quite believe" it.

Speaking to GamesRadar+ ahead of the Golden Joystick Awards 2026, the voice actor behind Monoco and Francois recalls Clair Obscur's trophy sweep "was such a fantastic time" last year. "I mean, I still couldn't quite believe that we were winning so many awards as we were winning them. I remember WhatsApping my wife going, 'Oh, we won the first one. Oh, we won the second one.'"

Even as Clair Obscur picked up award after award, Keeble says he "still wasn't expecting to win Game of the Year" - you know, the biggie. "And a year and a half on from the game coming out, people are still so in love with the game. You know, we 've been doing all these conventions. I went to New York, Rhode Island, Cyprus, did MCM London recently, and just the fans are still so in love with it. And it's just such a wonderful community. So I'm very, very lucky and privileged to be involved in such a game."

As you might recall, last year Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 managed to match Baldur's Gate 3's record by winning all five major GOTY awards. It won big at the fan-voted Golden Joystick Awards 2025, as well as the industry-led DICE, GDC and BAFTA awards. The game also took home gold at The Game Awards, which is determined by a combination of both fan and critic votes.

#3842. Embracer begin yet another round of layoffs at Crystal Dynamics, while they're still midway through development on two Tomb Raider games

Update: Studio confirms eight staff lost their jobs

Update 18/11: Crystal Dynamics have provided the following statement to RPS, confirming it cut eight staff members:

As initially reported by Vertical Slice (thanks, Chris!), the workforce of Tomb Raider studio Crystal Dynamics is being cut as part of a new set of layoffs by owners Embracer. As far as is currently known, those affected include senior game designer Joshua Mitchell, senior environment technical artist Kevin Baker, and UI software engineer Garin R. K. Richards, all of whom shared news of their redunancies on LinkedIn. There may be more affected, but neither Crystal Dynamics nor Embracer have offered comments on the reduction of staff as yet.

This now marks the studio's fifth round of layoffs since Embracer acquired it in 2022, following cuts in March 2025, August 2025, November 2025, and March this year. This is a drastic amount even considering the current state of the industry, with layoffs seemingly happening several times a week, but unfortunately, this is par for the course for Embracer. Even still, it makes one wonder just how many staff are left at Crystal Dynamics by now. Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis and Tomb Raider: Catalyst are still in production, so you'd hope that the studio won't be shuttered entirely.

According to Legacy of Atlantis' Steam page, generative AI has been used in the development of Legacy of Atlantis "to support some early exploration and temporary development content. Any AI-assisted assets were either replaced or refined by humans in order to maintain the creative and artistic vision of the development team." I would hope that this isn't a case of Embracer cutting staff in the misguided hope that they can just be replaced with the use of genAI, but who can say. Solidarity to those affected, who I hope can find new work soon.

#3841. Just how detailed is the audio in GTA 6? Well, even convenience store refrigerators "all have their own unique sounds", says Rockstar dev

If you've been online at all today, you'll know that what feels like the entire world is currently fawning over GTA 6. As the reviews dropped, one thing quickly became very clear: this is a game absolutely packed with detail. Our own Chris noted that, thanks to this focus on specific detail and unbelievable nuance, Grand Theft Auto 6 is "the most unbelievable video game world ever made". And it's no accident: this is something Rockstar put a lot of dedicated effort into.

It's been well-established that the studio has gone above and beyond to make this interactive world one of the most richly-developed we've ever seen: Rockstar has told us it "re-engineered" its weather systems to "achieve a sense of scale we haven't felt before," adding hurricanes, rainbows and heavy rain. It simulated and built a complex drug system, allowing Lucia and Jason to partake in drug use "directly from their inventory" and "at any time". But there are still details emerging from the dev team that are blowing my mind. And the most recent byte of information I saw was related to how Rockstar worked with sound.

"Much of the dynamic soundscape is informed by the incredibly detailed art throughout the world," explains Alastair MacGregor, vice president of audio at Rockstar. "One small example is that convenience store refrigerators all have their own unique sounds. In a run-down store, the refrigerators and freezers are loud and sound like they are badly maintained. Their compressor units can be heard mechanically whirring away from years of neglect. As a result, the bottles behind the doors can be heard shaking and the units click on and off more frequently. In an up-market store, the refrigerators are quieter, adding a subtle hum to the environment."

This level of detail is, quite frankly, absurd. It's a testament to granularity Rockstar is willing to go to in making Leonida feel truly lived-in and realistic. And this level of production isn't restricted to internal locations, either. "On the ambient side, we love the contrast between the manicured luxury islands, with the sizzle of crickets and lawn sprinklers backed by birdsong, yacht halyards clanging in the distance, and yard work going on, versus urban areas with the sounds of people living on top of each other - snatches of every genre of music, distant voices, cars peeling out, construction, the omnipresent hum of elderly air conditioners struggling with the humidity," continues MacGregor.

He goes on to say that if you're wandering the streets of Gellhorn - a coastal city in Kelly County on the western side of Leonida - it's acoustically a very different vibe than the high-rise centre of Vice City, where the sound bounces between the buildings. This means that the engine is handling not just the sounds of things as minute as bugs in the grass, but also how that sound travels, and interacts with other physical entities in the world. "We've spent years iterating on reverb technology to make sure that you can feel that - from the pops of cars backfiring to the wash of a helicopter passing by overhead to birds squawking in the trees," concludes MacGregor.

GTA 6 launches tomorrow - Thursday, 19th November - for PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. It's also worth noting that Rockstar has been embroiled in legal action after it was accused of union busting following the firing of over 30 employees. The case's conclusion will be determined this week.

Eight years on since the launch of its first chapter, Deltarune seems to be rapidly approaching completion. With five chapters already released for Toby Fox's sequel to the beloved RPG Undertale, two more are expected before the game is complete. And according to Deltarune creator Toby Box, not only is chapter 6 close to being finished, but work has also already begun on chapter 7.

Fox provided the status update in his most recent newsletter. Kicking off with a general note that chapter 6 is "progressing well", Fox explains that "the game is now a structurally complete draft that can be played from the beginning to the end. He further elaborates that "all the maps, events and battles exist", with the exception of one optional event that's still being worked on.

As a result, the Deltarune team is now at the point where they feel comfortable commencing localisation and preliminary testing. Fox clarifies, however, that full testing won't begin just yet, as "some important scenes and details are still undercooked in their presentation". Indeed, while chapter 6 is progressing rapidly, players shouldn't expect an imminent release. "Even though chapter 6 is a rather short chapter, I would like it to be as good as possible. I won't be able to rush this," Fox points out.

As for Chapter 7, Fox says that development has "only just started". Designers who have finished their Chapter 6 work have moved on to work on the new chapter, while Fox has shared some of the dialogue and events with the Deltarune team. "Just when the story reached a critical moment, I stopped reading. I told my team they need to complete more of the game before I tell them what happens," he explained, adding that "Everyone agrees it's more fun this way."

It's impressive progress, considering that chapter 5 released in June. Then again, development of Deltarune has accelerated rapidly since 2025, when Fox released chapters 3 and 4 of the game in the same year. The launch of chapter 5 also demonstrated just how much fans want to see the story through, as 300,000 concurrent players flocked to Steam to check out the latest chunk of the game.

A new Fallout game is indeed on the way, but it's not what you're expecting. Bethesda's next post-apocalyptic project is in fact a cat-themed hidden object game.

Earlier this week, a listing from the Australian Classifications Board accidentally spilled information about a game called A Wasteland Full of Cats. The now-deleted description let slip that it's a hidden object game - think Where's Wally/Waldo - where you need to find cats in some of the series' underground Vaults and the dangerous radioactive lands outside.

"You play as one of the cats in the Vault. One day there is an accident in the Vault and all of the cats who live there escape out into the Wasteland. It is up to you with the help of some NPCs you meet along the way to find them and return them to the Vault," according to the listing.

"This game has 14 locations, 33 rooms + a vault of recognizable levels from the Fallout franchise with light puzzle mechanics that uncover some hidden levels that aren't required to finish the game. There is a final boss fight where the player has to shoot some Rad roaches in order to save the last remaining cats and humans. This game will be part of Devcats 'Full of Cats' series of cats and plays like the other games in the series. This game is in partnership with Bethesda and the Fallout franchise."

It didn't take long for series owner Bethesda to confirm the leak, either. "Cat's out of the bag," the studio writes on social media, explaining that it's partnered with non-profit animal charity Dallas Pets Alive and developer Devcat Games on the "Fallout-inspired adventure."

There's no trailer or release date yet, but Bethesda says it'll "have more to share soon."

If finding hard-to-spot felines sounds like your vibe, Devcat Games has a ton of other games in the Full of Cats series, whether you're into exploring castles or flats or outer space.

A Wasteland Full of Cats might not be the Fallout game fans were expecting after the company formally announced remasters for Fallout 3 and Fallout: New Vegas, alongside a new game from Obsidian Entertainment, but it sounds like a cute stop over along the way. Fallout 5 is also in early pre-production.

#3838. Sony defeat $2.6 billion UK class action lawsuit which argued PlayStation's dominant market position fuels "excessive and unfair" game prices

It's a joyous day for lawyers representing plucky little game and console makers Sony. A UK class action lawsuit which accused the company of using the PlayStation Store's dominant market position to fuel "excessive and unfair" prices for digital games has been dismissed in its entirety by the Competition Appeal Tribunal in London.

As reported by Reuters and The Game Business, the body ruled that the lawsuit - brought by Alex Neill on behalf of folks who bought digital games on PlayStation between August 2016 and February 2026 - failed to establish that Sony had infringed competition law.

The lawsuit claimed that PlayStation's dominant position when it comes to selling digital games on its platforms via the PlayStation Store subjected consumers to "excessive and unfair prices", as a result of terms and a 30% commission fee levied against developers. Neill and co argued owning a PlayStation traps game buyers within a competitionless ecosystem, thereby impacting their ability to seek out a better deal.

It's quite similar to the arguments which have been made against Valve in similar lawsuits concerning the Steam overlords' dominance over the PC game buying space, though a key distinction is that there is some competition on PC via the likes of the Epic store and GOG. How effective some of that competition can be in practice is a different kettle of fish, but the options are there.

In a judgement that could potentially factor into the responses to any similar lawsuits against Valve or other PC storefronts going forwards, the tribunal ruled that Sony compete in a wider ‘systems market’ against Xbox, Nintendo and PC, with PlayStation having no legal duty under competition law to allow third-party stores onto their platform as competition closer to home. The latter the tribunal noted would be expensive, complex and come with potential security ramifications.

As if that wasn't enough, the body ruled that as far as the pricing being unfair went, Neill hadn't proven that Sony’s profit margins were excessive and declared there was no evidence the presence of rival storefronts on PlayStation would've seen prices come down. That's essentially the word NO written in the largest font possible on a sheet of paper the size of a table, then.

Every lawsuit's different, especially when filed in different countries, but if I was one of the other class action suits against Sony or another big game seller on the go at the moment, I'd maybe not be feeling so hot right now. On the other hand, perhaps seeing what the tribunal judged Neill not to have provided suffiencient evidence for might aid those other efforts in formulating their arguments ready to face the scrutiny of government bodies and corporate law-talkers.

The best parts of GTA 6 happen when everyone puts their guns away.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

GTA 6 has dragged us out of our comfort zone here at PC Gamer, forcing us to play a game on a console. A tragedy! But it's OK because GTA 6, as you may have heard, is rather good. And it's especially good when the shooting stops and you just get to hang out with your weird crime pals.

This seems to be the consensus among my colleagues in crime, who I've gathered to share their favourite parts of GTA 6's early game—fishing, interior decorating and chilling with some problematic faves.

I've been playing GTA since the top-down days, but with every new incarnation of Rockstar's criminal caper I've been drifting away from the action and learning to appreciate life in the slow lane. I have two wolves inside me, and in GTA 6, with its potent life sim DNA, the wolf who just wants to knock back beers with my virtual buddies is soundly beating the one who keeps screaming, "Do more crime!"

Guys, GTA 6 is a cosy game. It's a restorative holiday. I wake up and meditate with my partner before she goes to work. I do a bit of lifting. Watch some TV. Then it's time for a drive. Maybe I'll buy a new shirt or get a tasteful and definitely not monstrously-huge slab of ink to honour my son at the grotty tattoo parlour. Then the ocean beckons me—it's fishing time! I take some snaps of my catch so I can brag about it to my best friend. Oh, Brian is calling? He wants me to do more crimes? Sorry, Bri! I'm going treasure hunting in my boat and sending my partner thirst traps.

It's all just so pleasantly wholesome. Playing videogames with Cal, fixing up the house with Lucia, doing errands for my eccentric neighbour. Sure, that time I agreed to steal her best friend's mobility scooter definitely falls into the crime caper category, but only slightly. That's been my favourite chase so far—inching down the road while an old lady slowly jogs after me.

GTA's combat is serviceable and sometimes a whole lotta fun (I beat up some dudes with a basketball last night), and I've had a hoot getting stuck into Leonida's coke smuggling scene, but it feels like GTA's most impressive innovations are found in the quieter parts—the way it's constantly getting you to build relationships on your off hours, the wee nods to roleplaying, the believability and vibrancy of Leonida. This has been a crucial part of GTA since the San Andreas days, but in GTA 6 it feels like it's become the focus. I'm extremely happy about this.

GTA 6 has so many fun, small ways to make standing around and listening to dialogue more immersive that it almost makes the parts where you actually have to pick up a gun and shoot feel weirdly stagnant. I love the missions where you're just shooting the shit—building furniture, buying beers for a pal going through it, playing videogames. I love that I can do things like pour myself a coffee or light a cigarette while I'm having a conversation with another character. I love that I can construct a whole morning routine where I work out, go for a shower, and pick my outfit for the day.

The 'quieter' moments are where Leonida and its inhabitants really shine. I've lost track of how many times I've forgone a mission in favour of stopping to engage in all of the little random encounters—like a woman harassing a drive-thru worker for cheese, or a guy who is so lawsuit-brained that he ventures back into his burning vehicle for a bigger payday. Dilly-dallying has never felt so good.

GTA 6's fishing is pretty much unchanged from Red Dead Redemption 2, but I'm already doing it a lot more here because of Jason and Cal's ongoing fishing rivalry. We're catching somewhat big fish, sending pics, and talking trash about how the other guy will never find a bigger one.

It's wonderful and totally optional, which is indicative of how GTA 6 imbues many activities that would otherwise just 'be there' with social incentives. Every task, chore, or hobby involves talking to someone or sharing your day, and yes, it's pretty cosy. And if you're looking for a better fishing reel, check the sports shop near Jason's house.

I love when a game gives you a broad objective to just go earn money—also known as pulling a Baldur's Gate 2. It's a great excuse to diverge from the main path, to actually spend time getting to know a place without feeling pressured to progress the story in some meaningful way. In my last session, I spent most of my time exploring old shipwrecks for treasure—just me, my diving gear, some lost relics and the occasional shark.

Which, sure, it's an open world game with a lot of things to do on the side. This is not exactly a revelation. But, as always with Rockstar, the difference is in the production value and the attention to detail. The level of immersion is such that it doesn't feel like you're ticking off tasks on a checklist, because everything happens through the filter of Jason and Lucia's day-to-day. Every journey distracts you with surprising interactions and interesting things to check out. Every text message and social post builds the illusion of a place rich with life and detail. And so, yeah, when you finally decide to go do a main quest and the bullets start flying, it's almost disappointing to be back doing the things GTA has done for decades.

Finding and inputting GTA 6 safe codes is a slicker way to break into the 50+ safes scattered throughout the GTA 6 map. While some safes can be opened with sheer brute force, those that require a code often offer more lucrative rewards, so finding these safe codes can be a great way to make cash fast in GTA 6.

Unfortunately, these safe codes aren't always easy to come by. While some of the safe codes in GTA 6 are set – with those critical to the story and major side missions always consisting of the same digits– many of the codes are randomized and can change from player to player. So, while I can't give you the codes for those safes, I can at least help by guiding you on how to obtain them. So read on for tips on finding these randomized safe codes and for a list of set safe codes and their locations.

There are two methods of getting GTA 6 safe codes:

Which you'll need depends on the location, but by using your Focus by pressing down on L3 and R3/LS and RS, you can highlight the location of the safe code if there is one. If you can't see one, you probably need to threaten the staff by holding down the LT/L2 button and then press X/Square to threaten. Eventually, the threaten option will turn into a 'Safe code?' option, as seen in the image above. The Avery Pawn Shop GTA 6 safe code is an example of one of these, so why not use that to try it out.Alternatively, safes that require a code can be blown open using sticky bombs. These are only unlocked once you reach the Credit Checked mission in Chapter 3, but as I've explained in my dedicated guide to getting into the Kingpin Bowling safe in GTA 6, there are a few you can pick up at the alley - and presumably other places around Leonida - before you unlock them at Ammu-Nation.

These are the set GTA 6 safe codes that are the same for every player:

Aside from the 0420 safe code that's given to you in Chapter 1, there are three main safe codes you'll need when gathering funds in GTA 6, and they're all related to the Kolt gang in Port Gellhorn. All three codes are found in the same place, Brooks Boatworks, but since they're set, you can use them from our list above without having to go looking for them. This won't save you a lot of trouble, though, as you'll still have to get past the gang in all three locations anyway.

#3834. Only two days out from GTA 6, its publisher Take-Two lay off staff at XCOM and Civilization developer Firaxis

About a third of the workforce has been cut, reportedly

Upsettingly, it is that time of the week again, as Take-Two are laying off staff at Firaxis, the developer behind Civilization and XCOM, only a little over a year the last time the studio suffered from layoffs. Firaxis are, notably, owned by Take-Two, the publisher of GTA 6 which comes out in, oh, two days time? Interesting timing, 'ey.

Word of the layoffs came from Bloomberg, who report that about 60 people are losing their jobs, apparently roughly a third of its staff. The studio's head, Heather Hazen, is also leaving. A spokesperson for 2K Games (the Take-Two label that manages Firaxis) shared a statement on the layoffs: "Firaxis is restructuring and recentering around the studio’s core strength - designing world class strategy games that have set the industry standard for the genre for the last 30 years.

"As part of these changes, the size of the studio is being reduced to focus on design, technology and the player experience, which means saying goodbye to talented colleagues who helped build Firaxis. These decisions are never easy, but they’re essential to build the next chapter of Firaxis." I don't feel personally confident in the idea that the only way to make a company succeed is by laying a bunch of people off thereby making it much harder to make anything in the first place, especially in the lead-up to what will likely be the best selling game of the decade, but what do I know!

Bloomberg also report Firaxis have been working on a new XCOM, which is yet to be announced, but the project has apparently had to contend with numerous development issues, missing a "significant milestone over the summer." This new XCOM game hasn't been cancelled at the very least, but anonymous sources that spoke with Bloomberg said it may have to deal with a shakeup due to the cuts. As always, solidarity with all those affected by this situation.

#3833. GTA 6 breaks the all-time livestream viewer record hours before it's available to play for most of the world

Hours before it's even playable in most of the world, Grand Theft Auto 6 has already broken the record for the most viewers across livestreaming platforms like Twitch.

According to streaming data and analytics website Streams Charts, GTA 6 had amassed 6.38m live viewers across Twitch, YouTube, and Kick at 12:30 UTC today. At that time, the game had been officially available for a few hours in New Zealand, and elsewhere by using a region-switch trick.

The previous record for most live viewers was set by Valorant, Riot Game's popular tactical shooter, during its closed beta in xx. That game brought in 1.74m live viewers, but it's worth noting there was a promotion offering players a chance to access the beta if they watched a stream. Despite having no such incentive, GTA 6 has more than tripled Valorant's record.

Twitch is the largest platform for GTA 6 streams according to Streams Charts, and already the game is the 6th biggest category in Twitch history. It's also expected the figure will increase as GTA 6 launches officially in more regions of the world.

If you'd like to find out when exactly Grand Theft Auto 6 releases for you, check out Eurogamer's GTA 6 launch time guide for an accurate list by country. You can also read the Everything We Know about Grand Theft Auto 6 guide for a full breakdown on all the details ahead of its launch in your region.

The GTA 6 Bowling Alley safe code is rather difficult to find when you undertake the Hit Kingpin Bowling mission in Chapter 2 and rob the place, though you can hit it earlier as just Lucia. This is because the code isn't actually in the bowling alley at all.

First thing's first, the code you want is 0300. Like many other robbery safe codes, this one isn't randomised, and will crack open the safe, netting you about $3,400. Make sure to also steal the unique Gutterland Moreland 850 shotgun from the pool table in the main room.

Now, if you wanted to find the code yourself, it's actually located in Brooks Boatworks, another Kolt & Associates gang hideout in the northwest of Port Gellhorn.

You actually visit the boatworks with the doctor and Dunk during the Slam Dunk mission. Looking at the map on the wall to also get the safe codes for the La Cascara Motel and Brooks Boatworks itself, the other Kolt & Associate robberies in Port Gellhorn.

These are all pretty lucrative in terms of money and narcotics that you can then sell to Dunk once you unlock his stash box.

#3830. Blade Runner 2099 showrunner turned to Ridley Scott to answer canon questions: "I needed the Bible for our show"

Join the GamesRadar community for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

Ridley Scott is the closest thing to Blade Runner's loremaster

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Blade Runner 2099 is set 80 years after the events of 1982 sci-fi classic Blade Runner, but despite the Replicant-filled world undergoing some radical changes in the intervening decades, the Prime Video show's creator turned to Ridley Scott for clarification on a number of canon questions.

Scott, of course, directed Blade Runner and is an executive producer on Blade Runner 2099. So when 2099 showrunner Silka Luisa had questions about the history of the cyberpunk world, there was only one place to turn. "He's such an idol for me. It was like meeting a rock star," Luisa tells GamesRadar+. "He had so much insight into the first film, because so much of it is off-screen your imagination just takes over, but there's a lot of open questions intentionally, right? It's very ambiguous.

"So when I went to go write," Luisa continues. "I realized that the canon is not concrete, and so it's hard to build on top of that foundation when you're not sure if what you're saying is accurate or not. And so, what was really helpful with Ridley was being able to ask him: What I thought this meant – is this correct? What did you think Off-world was? Where did you think the Replicants came from? Tell me about Tyrell; how did you imagine him? I mean, just as a fan, they're the questions you would be dying to have answered. But also from a practical sense, as a writer, I just needed to know. I needed the Bible for our show, and that was Ridley."

This makes sense – Scott is perhaps the only person to have played a major creative role in all three live-action Blade Runner projects, as he was also an executive producer on 2017's Denis Villeneuve-directed Blade Runner 2049. And unlike Star Wars, Game of Thrones, the MCU, and many storytelling sandboxes, there is no one person or group that is the arbiter of canon in the Blade Runner universe. Instead, it's up to the creators of each individual project to forge ahead, which could become a problem when looking back.

It's safe to say, then, that Blade Runner 2099 will have one eye on the past, while looking to the future. Starring Michelle Yeoh as Replicant Olwen, and Hunter Schafer as a human Cora, Blade Runner 2099 is set in the aftermath of a Replicant revolt that saw synthetic humans rise to power and humans subjugated. Bad news for Cora, who must go undercover at the LAPD to win freedom for her and her brother. The final trailer is out now.

While it's not ignoring canon, we do know that Blade Runner 2099 is "not directly connected" to Blade Runner 2049, and won't directly pick up on the events of that movie, as it's designed to "stand alone". And while a second season of Blade Runner 2099 is unlikely, as the 8-episode show is already being billed as a "limited series", franchise producers Alcon Entertainment have suggested a AAA Blade Runner video game is in the works.

Blade Runner 2099 releases in full on Prime Video on November 25. For more, here's our Blade Runner timeline, and our breakdown of the most exciting new TV shows.

#3829. GTA 6 is so big, it managed to break Reddit - and it isn't even actually out yet

Grand Theft Auto 6 isn't even out yet, and it's already causing some technical issues over at the game's official Reddit page.

In a post verified by r/GTA6 moderators and pinned to the page, user and moderator PapaXah wrote "GTA 6 broke Reddit", and explained that "many things" were currently busted at the time of the post. Looking through Reddit, many flairs (little labels attached to posts) aren't loading properly and appear as a string of code rather than proper images. PapaXah also replied to one user suggesting they make real flairs based on these busted flairs, writing: "Reddit's so broken I couldn't even do it. We actually have a bunch of new flairs that I can't even upload."

Another moderator, TekS, also acknowledged that some user's posts may not be viewable as a result of ongoing strain on Reddit during GTA 6's release. They commented: "If you can't post/comment or see your user flair, well, know that it's perfectly normal."

Ahead of the game's full launch across the world, the Grand Theft Auto 6 has already broken viewership records across streaming platforms like Twitch and YouTube. Interesting details about the game are also trickling out, including the fact that different refrigerators have their own unique sounds. Video games, ladies and gentlemen.

With Grand Theft Auto 6 releasing today, our review has been released to the wild with it. It is overwhelmingly positive, with Chris Tapsell dubbing GTA 6 as "the most believable and unbelievable video game world ever made" and rated it a full five stars.

#3828. What would Rockstar have done if GTA hadn't taken off? Former tech director Obbe Vermeij on Scottish zombies, James Bond and the "curse" of success

"We ended up just cutting and cutting it."

It's bizarre today to think of Rockstar working on games that aren't Grand Theft Auto. Frankly, it's bizarre to think of Rockstar working on games that aren't GTA 6, which rolls onto console hard drives this week. A decade in the making, with a development team of thousands scattered across an international network of studios, GTA 6 aims to be the Maximum Game. It's both a dense, lively open world and a monument to the exhausting impersonality of "triple-A" game productions. It contains multitudes: birdlife! Realistic cloud formation! Fuel mechanics! Romance! Soda visibly sloshing around in bottles! It's an imperial production shadowed by labour disputes, that appears to have given Rockstar's various teams little time or space to think about anything else.

It wasn't ever thus. Once upon a time, Rockstar weren't just known for GTA and to a considerably lesser extent, Red Dead Redemption. Once upon a time, they had a reputation for slightly dodgy experiments. I recently interviewed former Rockstar North tech director Obbe Vermeij about a few of them, including Agent, the unofficial James Bond game Rockstar toyed with before putting all chips on Grand Theft Auto 5.

During the noughties especially, when the most expensive games took considerably less time to make, Rockstar tried their hand at a number of projects besides GTA. There was 2002's Manhunt, a rancid parody of snuff films – not much loved, but sufficiently admired to spawn a sequel in the hands of Rockstar London. There was 2005's adaptation of Walter Hill flick The Warriors - a mouthy Homeric beat 'em up in which you cross New York on foot over the course of a single night - and 2006's Rockstar Presents Table Tennis - an inexplicable pivot towards realistic sports simulation from Rockstar San Diego. Later in 2006 came Bully, aka Canis Canem Edit, a boarding school life sim from Rockstar Vancouver (née Barking Dog Studios). I didn't warm to Bully, myself, but I've never been able to get its sardonic OST out of my head.

In amongst all these, Rockstar weighed up several game projects that never made it out of the building. The aforesaid Agent is perhaps the best-known, but my conversation with Vermeij (who worked at Rockstar from 1995 to 2009) began with "Z", a fleeting attempt to expand into the world of zombie action games, which Rockstar spent a few weeks mulling over in the wake of Grand Theft Auto: Vice City. It was set in the islands of Scotland, which would have made it the only Rockstar North project to unfold in the studio's backyard. "I think it was meant to be smaller than GTA, map-wise, and there weren't going to be any deserted cities - it was really just islands and some villages," Vermeij told me. "But it really didn't get that far."

The pitch for Z couldn't be further from the sweat and glitter of GTA 6's Miami, but the two projects would have shared a taste for 'simulation' elements. "It actually was going to have cars running out of fuel," Vermeij told me. "That was going to be one of the things, and the whole idea was that you'd find cars and they'd only have a little bit of fuel in them." As for why Z never entered full development, turns out desolate North Atlantic archipelagos full of corpses can be a bit of a downer. "Everybody was super excited to do something new," Vermeij went on. "And then pretty quickly, we kind of realised that it's really just a depressing version of GTA, and it sort of died."

The increasing success of Grand Theft Auto during these years was something of a "curse", Vermeij went on. It meant that a lot of Rockstar's ventures beyond GTA were eventually folded back into the series. "It's very difficult to have a studio and have one mega game, and then do something on the side," he explained. "It's almost impossible, because at any time during the development of the smaller project, management's going to say 'oh! The big project's in trouble. We need more people.' And they're just going to pull everybody from that small team onto the big team, so even if we had progressed with [Z], what would have happened is we would have had to start GTA 4 at the same time, and eventually the small team would just be merged with the big team again."

Rockstar's Bondalike game Agent got a lot further down the road to release than Z. It was in development for several years following GTA 4's launch, and was touted by co-founder Sam Houser as Rockstar's next megagame. "A lot of work had been done on that," Vermeij recalled. "And then we ended up just cutting and cutting it, because the same thing happened – at some point you kind of go OK, well, we better get on with the next GTA."

Agent sounds like it could have been a hoot, at least going by Vermeij's description of his own time with the project. It was a relatively linear, level-based action game with a touch of camp. "There was a French ski resort, and there was going to be a Mediterranean town like San Tropez, somewhere like that," Vermeij explained. "There was going to be a North African place, like Morocco or Egypt. The last level was going to be on the moon, with lasers – like Moonraker. There was another one, London or something, I can't remember. But then we just ended up cutting everything down, because what we could see happening was that at some point, we would have to go back to work on GTA. It wasn't close to being finished."

While never a spoof in the vein of Austin Powers, Agent would have been a sillier production than the grimy and downbeat GTA 4. "It was meant to lean into all the cliches," Vermeij said. "It was like James Bond from the 1970s - there was a girl with white boots. It wasn't a comedy, it was just completely over-the-top cliched."

As for the choice of a level-based format, this came from a desire for variety the studio couldn't realistically achieve in a GTA-style open world. "If you had to have them all on one map, you would basically have had to model a mini version of Europe," Vermeij said, "So you couldn't do that." Players might have been able to revisit locations containing several missions, which calls to mind Io Interactive's later Hitman: World of Assassination games, to say nothing of their own bash at the Flemingverse, 007 First Light. "I don't how whether it was going to be completely linear, or whether you were always going to be able to visit all those locations." Vermeij said.

Needless to say, Rockstar's Bondalike would have featured chase scenes. Vermeij himself worked on the moving parts. "I remember doing some work on what we called the car recording stuff for GTA," he went on. "So if a level designer wanted to set up a chase scene, they would drive one car, record it, and then play back the recording, drive a second car and record that... and so driving one by one, you could set up a whole chase scene. I did a version of that for [human] characters as well, because for one of the Agent missions in the French ski resort, there was like a chase where the bad guys were on skiis and using their machine guns. So I set up a thing where you'd play them one by one, and then play the whole thing back. There was maybe like five or six bad guys and they'd ski after you, and then it was just up to the player to avoid them."

According to Vermeij, Agent never had a defined story during his time with it. It was more of a mix of scenario concepts, "kind of how we used to do games with GTA 3 and Vice City". Mind you, the absence of a nailed-down plot isn't necessarily a sign that Agent was lightyears from being finished. Even at their most byzantine, Bond movie plotlines often feel like an afterthought. "It's like oh yeah, there's a bad guy and there's a thingally-dingally that needs to be captured before the world comes to an end," summarised Vermeij. Still, Agent would spend a long time in limbo after Vermeij left. It's still unclear how much it was in active development before Rockstar's trademark finally evaporated in November 2018.

One thing I learned while reading up on Rockstar's checkered history was that GTA 3, the game that made GTA a Thing on PlayStation, wasn't deemed an immediate hit at launch. According to Vermeij himself, it was months before Rockstar realised what they'd built. This inspired an obvious closing question: what might Rockstar have done, if GTA 3 hadn't blown up the way it did? Which of those other projects might have become the focus?

"I really have never thought about it," Vermeij pondered. "When Rockstar San Diego joined, it was 2002, and they already had a bunch of games and a bunch of franchises, like Midnight Club and Smuggler's Run. They were already into driving games and city games in that way, so it wouldn't have surprised me if we'd gone in that direction anyway. But then they were more about car modding and decals and stuff like that.

"At Rockstar North, we only had Manhunt and GTA," he went on. "With Manhunt, that team was in development hell for a while, they had a couple of rough years where they got stuck and in the end, they pulled through, and they got a pretty decent game. But I don't think that would have been the future. I don't think [Rockstar North] would have done a Manhunt 2. So yeah, it would be Table Tennis, I think! Everything on Table Tennis!"

The amount of time it takes to develop games has been growing steadily longer for decades, and Atlus' Persona series is no exception to this rule. While Persona 4 Golden and Persona 5 were separated by four years (long considered standard for game development) it's been seven years since Persona 5 Royal and Persona 6 still doesn’t have a release date—though we did get Metaphor: ReFantazio in between.

Nonetheless, it's an issue that P-Studio is very much aware of, and it was recently addressed by general producer Kazuhisa Wada. In an interview with Sega Samania (via Eurogamer) Wada stressed that the wait for whatever comes after Persona 6 will be shorter.

"Persona 6 is not the end," Wada explained. "We have been working to make sure that people won't have to wait as long for the next game as they have previously. In order for Persona to grow as an IP, we consider how to live up to people's expectations in terms of creativity and development every day."

Now, we're probably not looking at a dramatic reduction in development time. Wada emphasised that "large-scale RPGs like the Personal series can take five years or more to develop," adding that. "There can be a long time between numbered entries." Yet even if the average timeline was five years, that would be a considerable improvement.

Wada doesn't explain how Atlus plans to speed up development of its games. But there's always one question when developers begin talking about making games quicker—does it involve generative AI? Wada expressed interest in the tech several years ago, stating that it might be useful for "early concept and idea formation" and that the Atlus art team had been "talking about wanting to implement AI." That said, there's been little, if any talk about AI from Atlus since, and there's no evidence at present that Persona 6 uses the tech.

In fact, Atlus hasn't said much about Persona 6 at all since the game was announced earlier this year, though there are rumours that we'll find out more at The Game Awards in a few weeks' time. As for Wada, while he didn't comment on Persona 6 in detail, he did say that Atlus is "creating something better than anything we've made before, and that is hugely satisfying."

The GTA 6 Tourist Trap mission is a very important one as it's the beginning of the end of Chapter 1. Without getting into major spoilers just yet, it's fair to say that things go a bit wrong in this mission, and it's all completely unavoidable. That makes it a very linear mission, but it's not always clear where you should be going in all the chaos, so my walkthrough for the Tourist Trap mission in GTA 6 will help you out.

I've kept this guide as spoiler-free as possible, but this is a major moment in GTA 6's story, so you've been warned!

First of all, if you're yet to even start Tourist Trap, make sure you check my list of things to do before Tourist Trap in GTA 6 so that you miss out on as little as possible in Chapter 1.

To get Tourist Trap started, head over to the Lucia icon in the park in the south of Key Lento. A cutscene plays showing Lucia and Jason getting picked up by Mattia and Kat and then driving over to the Grassrivers Vistor Center for a job – retrieve the bag in locker 17 on the second floor. Once you gain control of Jason, here's what you do:

You'll eventually get ambushed by undercover cops and cannot fight back – as far as I'm aware, there's no way to avoid this. Soon after, there's a moment where you must move Jason towards a chair at the interview table, and then it's back into some cutscenes. It all eventually breaks out into a cop-versus-dirty-cop shootout, giving Jason and Lucia a chance to escape:

Once you get to Cal's house, that's the end of Tourist Trap. It's quite a simple mission overall as there are a lot of scripted elements and you've just got to do what the game tells you, with your only real choice being whether you kill or wound all the cops you face. Anyway, once the cutscene with Jason, Lucia, and Cal is over, it's onto the next mission, Home Sweet Home, and eventually Chapter 2.

#3824. Archetype go all in on the Mass Effect vibes with a FemJun reveal, but I'm just left hoping they'll call the alternative option MascJun to balance it out

I know it, you know it, hell, I'm sure developer Archetype Entertainment know it: Exodus is kind of just Mass Effect again. That's in part because the DNA of the game has been built by series vets like Drew Karpyshyn, Chad Robertson and James Ohlen. But it's also because, well, they're putting FemShep in the game. Yes, I'm being a tad facetious here, but when the latest trailer for your game is literally titled "Female Jun Reveal," well, comparisons will be made!

To top it all off, a blog post from the devs literally refers to the alternate gender for the protag as FemJun. They know what they're doing. In any case, first up, her voice actor! She's being played by Carina Conti, an up and comer last digitally heard in Mafia: The Old Country as Isabella Torrisi. Male Jun (who hasn't been given a nickname, which couldn't possibly serve to other female Jun (and MascJun is right there!)) has also had his voice actor confirmed as Stephen Oyoung, who you'll have heard as Mister Negative in Insomniac's Spider-Man games and Red Hood in Gotham Knights.

It's been previously confirmed that no matter which gender you pick for Jun, you'll be able to romance whoever you like, so, happy smoochin'! The story will stay the same too, as will dialogue options, though I'm imagine some pronoun switcheroos will take place somewhere along the line.

I'm mostly just left feeling that this doesn't really seem like it'll fix the game's boring hero problem. Edwin made note of Jun's quite lacklustre vibe earlier this year, aptly tearing down MascJun's Instagram visage, though this was prior to the face model and voice actor change the character has undergone. Personally, I'm not sure that'll be enough, and FemJun kind of matches that Instagram look; the perfect bun and bangs that pop out when she takes her helmet off is quite silly too. Ah well! A game isn't done until it's done (which, in theory, will be April 7th next year).

#3823. All 34 of the infamously fired Rockstar staff appear in GTA 6 game credits, though some aren't listed as "former employees", curiously

UPDATE: The final few names have been confirmed.

UPDATE 19TH NOVEMBER: All of the 34 fired Rockstar employees appear in the credits for GTA 6. We were able to confirm the final few names' existence there after Rockstar posted the full credits online - in searchable form. Before this, the process of cross-checking was intensely laborious: it required watching a scrolling list of names for an hour-and-a-half to see if they appeared.

Also, we couldn't identify six names in the "former employees" section of the credits before because they don't appear there, we now know. These names appear listed under the departments the people worked for, as if they still worked at Rockstar. Why this is, we don't know - perhaps it's something to do with being involved in the employment tribunal or not. We're asking Rockstar for clarification.

ORIGINAL STORY 18TH NOVEMBER: Eurogamer can confirm that at least 28 of the 34 employees fired by Rockstar roughly a year ago - in an action that directly led to the employment tribunal Rockstar is currently facing in Scotland - are named in the credits of Grand Theft Auto 6.

A number of those fired employees are seeking compensation for unfair dismissal amid allegations of "union busting", in an employment tribunal that comes to an end today. The delayed climax of the case couldn't be more fateful, aligned as it is with tomorrow's release of GTA 6, and the outcome will be historic either way.

Rockstar recently revealed that more than 4,711 people worked at the company making GTA 6, employed across 12 offices around the world - a staff-count that has more than doubled since Red Dead Redemption 2. It's a game that's wowed critics - Eurogamer awarded GTA 6 five stars in our review this afternoon - and which observers expect to generate $2bn in revenue in its opening weekend alone.

But perhaps Christian Donlan put it best when digesting the opulence on display in the Netflix 'extended look' GTA 6 trailer. "To spend all this money making something so beautifully rich and detailed, to pay billions for this game and sweat every little animation, to float it out to us on Netflix, amongst genuine discussion around whether Netflix can handle it? That's commitment," he wrote. "And if you're willing to do that, and willing to do that to tell an underdog story, you should let your workers who made everything form a union."

#3822. Saihate Station: Twilight Edition announced for Switch

Publisher PLAYISM and developer viv have announced Saihate Station: Twilight Edition, a Switch version of the 2D exploration horror adventure game including the base game and downloadable content “Twilight Railway,” as well as two mini-games. It will launch on March 25, 2027 worldwide with English, Japanese, Korean, Traditional Chinese, and Simplified Chinese language support. A physical edition will be available in Japan for 8,800 yen.

Saihate Station first launched for PC via Steam on March 7, 2025. The downloadable content “Twilight Railway” launched on April 18, 2025.

Here is an overview of the game, via PLAYISM:

Since its release in March 2025, this 2D exploration horror adventure game has recorded a cumulative series total of 1.6 million downloads, an exceptional achievement for an indie free game, and continues to receive passionate support from fans in Japan and abroad. Now it is finally coming to Nintendo Switch!

Saihate Station: Twilight Edition includes the main game, the downloadable content “Twilight Railway,” and two mini-games, all in one package.

“After falling asleep on the last train, I woke up in a bizarre place called Saihate Station…”

Haru Akinashi is a self-effacing office worker who lacks confidence and fails at everything he tries. Having slept through his stop on the last train, he finds himself trapped in a bizarre place called Saihate Station, where gruesome supernatural phenomena occur.

Shion Tatsunami is his complete opposite: a cheerful, talented colleague and former friend—happens to be there as well, and the two promise to work together to return home.

Their interactions are awkward at first, given the estrangement, but with each problem they overcome together, Haru recalls their former friendship, and their bond grows stronger than before.

The main game features four multiple-ending story routes. The ending branches based on fluctuations in Haru’s “dependency level,” which changes according to the player’s actions.

Starting November 20, pre-orders for the physical edition will begin sequentially at retailers in Japan. As a first-print bonus, a “shaka-shaka acrylic stand keychain” featuring a train and character motif will be included. A limited edition featuring a special box with an “exclusive newly drawn mini-game book” and a “Haru-Shion handkerchief” is also planned. Bonuses and limited editions are available in limited quantities, so please place your pre-order early.

You'll be able to start looking for GTA 6 Transgressor locations after you complete the Thrillbillies mission in Chapter 2 and collect the Vapid Dominator from Wyman (if you have the Ultimate Edition, that is).

He'll text to ask for help finding old wrecked Transgressors he can use to restore the classic car, which you'll then get to drive. There are three of these junks located around Port Gellhorn which you'll have to scan with the WAiNK It app.

The first wrecked Transgressor you can find is in a trailer park north of Sarena's Bargain Store in the middle of Port Gellhorn (you might have to zoom in to see the store). Head north, cross the road, and jump over the wall to find it there.

The second wrecked Transgressor is further north in the garage of the house opposite the Kolt & Associate's Stash House robbery (there's a metal sunflower standing in the garden, which makes it easier to recognise.) It's also to the east of Brook's Boatworks and the west of Wasteland Offroad. Head around the side of the house via the driveway to find the car in an open garage at the back.

This last one is nice and easy, behind the Dirt Merchants mod shop in the south of Port Gellhorn. Simply head right via the track that leads behind the shop, following the fence on your right and then turn left to find the wreck at the back behind the kind of trailer park area.

Once you have all three cars scanned, Wyman will take a little time to assemble it, and then call you asking to Buck him some money. Open the app, select the payment requests option, and then pay him the $1,500 for the car. This will give you a quest marker to collect it from his scrapyard.

#3820. Mondrayn is a putrid, crunchy pixel art RPG about escaping from limbo where "dying doesn't mean the end of your suffering"

Everything's a bit grim these days, so let's just go all in on the misery shall we? Let's start with this line from the game's Steam page we'll be talking about today: "Mondrayn is a grim JRPG with survival elements where dying doesn't mean the end of your suffering." Crikey! You're telling me the sweet release of death won't be so saccharine after all? Sounds rough, so it's a good thing Mondrayn looks so darn compelling.

The world of Mondrayn is a dead one. You start out waking up in a city, it's in a gnarly state, of course, overrun by a disease of unknown origin. Horrible monsters are roaming about the place, cults are performing nasty rituals, and you've got no memories, so all you can do is try and make any friends you can, kill the undead and get out of, all places, limbo.

Mondrayn is an RPG in the sense that it utilises turn-based combat, "intertwined with shootouts." I'm not entirely sure how that manifests, you do seem to be able to do both regular attacks and special moves, the state of characters seems to have an impact, but truthfully I don't mind not understanding because what I'm here for are the utterly, delectably rancid vibes on display.

Every single pixel in this game looks like it was dipped in a vat of grime, puss, blood and vomit, and I revel in it! The enemy portraits are crunchy and violet, they look ripped straight out of some obscure art book for a Warhammer-esque tabletop game no one has ever heard of. It looks a bit fantasy, a bit steampunk, and incredibly, incredibly grimdark. It's the kind of world I'd rather instantly top myself than spend a second longer in, so, kudos to the fictional characters in it that have no choice in the matter for managing better than me. As it stands, Mondrayn has no release date, but you can wishlist it on Steam in the meantime.

#3819. PSA: Some GTA 6 Ultimate Edition content is only available for the first chapter, and you'll have to put in hard graft to unlock more

GTA 6's Ultimate Edition has proven enormously popular, despite its hefty $100 price tag. So much so that Strauss Zelnick, boss of Rockstar parent company Take-Two, recently confirmed it's the edition most people are buying - and that's despite a lack of specific information about how its unlockable content works. With GTA 6 just hours away from release, however - and out now in certain parts of the work - details are beginning to emerge, and the answer is perhaps a little surprising.

As previously confirmed, the $100/£90 Ultimate Edition provides access to exclusive vehicles, weapons, shops, and more, with the full list as follows:

Rockstar also previously revealed that "Ultimate Edition bonuses become available to Jason and Lucia across their story, with new items uncovered behind each chapter". The specifics of how - and when - all this stuff unlocks, though, remained unclear. So if you've opted for the Ultimate Edition, you might be wondering where your stuff is when you finally fire up the game. As reported by IGN, which has full unlock details, it turns out virtually all of GTA 6's Ultimate Edition content, as per details in the in-game shop, requires progressing through the main story - in some cases dozens and dozens of hours into the story - before it'll become available.

Ultimate Edition-exclusive shops, for instance, unlock during Chapter 1, and many of the other additions become available by the end of Chapter 2. That doesn't sound too difficult, but as Eurogamer's Chris Tapsell notes, reaching that point could take upward of 25 hours. As for some of the late-game unlocks, such as the Shitzu Squalo and the Vice City Style outfits and tattoos (available in Chapter 4) and Chapter 5's 95 Grotti Cheetah, you could be looking at closing in on 60 hours of playtime before they unlock.

"It'll vary depending how hard people focus on the main story," Chris explains, "but if you were mostly focused on the main story plus the optional character-based missions in largely chronological order, that's about how long it'd take."

It's also worth noting - perhaps surprisingly - that some Ultimate Edition content is only a temporary unlock, usable only during specific chapters. Jason's Dinka Enduro motorcycle and Crest Kayak, for instance, can only be accessed and enjoyed during Chapter 1. That's also true for his retro Vapid Ganado, available from the Coastal Auto Care mod shop in Key Lento. So basically, you'll want to make the most of these while you can!

All this might be a little disappointing for players who were expecting to be showered with Ultimate Edition spoils from the off (and that they'd be permanent unlocks), but the good news is 60 hours in GTA 6 is far from a chore. As Chris explained in his five star GTA 6 review, Rockstar's latest is an "irreducible mix of silliness, intimacy, grand ideas and rock 'n' roll action" that "pushes back the horizon of video games once again".

#3818. Witch on the Holy Night now available for iOS, Android in Japan

Publisher Aniplex and developer TYPE-MOON have released visual novel Witch on the Holy Night for iOS via App Store and Android via Google Play in Japan for 2,900 yen.

Witch on the Holy Night has previously been released for PlayStation 4, Switch, and PC via Steam. Shipments and digital sales have surpassed 500,000 units worldwide.

The mobile release coincides with the Witch on the Holy Night anime movie produced by ufotable, which debuted in Japanese theaters today.

Here is an overview of the game, via Aniplex:

Experience a young adult tale, set in the vibrant and bustling 1980s, that follows an innocent young man and two young “witches.”

Updates added since the original PC version include the fully voiced characters that fans have long awaited, as well as visuals remastered in full HD, bringing the experience to life with unparalleled image quality.

Various new visual elements not only imbue battle scenes with tension, but also breathe life into the characters’ everyday activities, with motions that bring a sense of animation and make the text even more deeply immersive.

Two witches dwell within a mansion atop a hill.

It is the late 1980s, the twilight years of a vibrant and bustling era. A boy arrives in the city only to encounter two witches living in the present day.

The boy leads a normal life. One of the girls is proud and dignified. The other lives hidden away, as if in slumber.

Three stars in parallel orbit, fated never to meet. The story of how these three completely different characters come to live under one roof will soon be revealed…

First released in 2012 for PC, Witch on the Holy Night returns after 10 years, further refined with fully voiced characters and a full high-definition visual remaster.

You won't find the GTA 6 pawn shop safe code by looking around, so here's how to get it

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you're looking around for the GTA 6 pawn shop safe code while being shot, deafened by alarms, and pressured by nearing sirens, you might be looking in the wrong place. This is a safe code you won't find lying around on a post-it note, and you'll have to interrogate some GTA 6 NPCs instead, so here's what you need to know about getting into the pawn shop safe.Keep in mind that this guide refers to the Avery Pawn shop, as there are other pawn shops around Leonida. Of the others we've heisted so far, none have had safes that require a code, but I'll update this guide if that changes!

To get the code for the GTA 6 pawn shop safe, you need to threaten the staff, who will eventually give it up, though they might also open fire on you, so be careful not to kill them all before you get the code.To threaten the staff, hold LT/L2, then press X/Square. After a couple of goes, the prompt should turn from 'Threaten' to 'Safe Code?' - but only after you've seen the safe. This means the best way to tackle this is actually to enter through the back of the building, check out the safe, then threaten the staff. If you do go through the front, just make sure you keep someone alive until you've been to the office, but there should be someone out the back anyway.

However you do it, the alarm will go off, so you'll need to head to the office to turn it off at the wall. This is also where the safe is, so you'll be heading there anyway.

You can still open the safe without the code, as long as you have a sticky bomb to hand. This is a much easier and quicker way to get the safe open - especially if you're a little heavy on your trigger finger. You can buy sticky bombs from Ammu-Nation after you've completed the Credit Check mission in Chapter 3, or you can pick some up from the Kingpin bowling alley, where you'll also find the GTA 6 bowling alley safe.

I did this twice, entering through the front the first time. Threatening the staff caused them to open fire on me, which led to a bit of chaos and a few bodies on the floor before I had to bail. The second time, I entered through the back, knocked down the first member of staff, entered the office, and then still had staff members making their way through from the front who succumbed to my threats. It's much easier this way - and you'll also be able to disable the alarm quicker, too.

For other GTA 6 safe codes, we've got a separate guide, and you should also take a look at our guide to stealing the secret GTA 6 Fast and Furious car while you're feeling criminal.

Welcome to Dungeon Master, PC Gamer's regular RPG column, where Online Editor Fraser Brown delves into PC gaming's most beloved and enduring genre. Grab a seat in our badly-lit tavern and please ignore the goblin puke.

I will probably be in the ground when Bethesda finally releases The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel—which is kind of liberating. I have hype immunity. But what's even more liberating is the fact that there's already an RPG that does everything I want from an Elder Scrolls game—2025's Tainted Grail: The Fall of Avelon.

Tainted Grail is unabashedly created in the mould of The Elder Scrolls, in that it is a primarily first-person fantasy RPG where flexibility is its superpower. You chart your own course and effectively construct your class, enhancing skills by using them as much as possible. But it is not merely the Elder Scrolls we have at home—it captures the very best that this kind of RPG can offer, and in some ways manages to outdo Bethesda.

This is apparent right from the get-go. In classic Elder Scrolls form, Tainted Grail begins with you banged up in a facility that incarcerates and studies unfortunates afflicted with a magical plague, of which you are one. Follow the critical path and you will meet a new friend, get in some tough fights and then escape.

By the time I finally escaped the island and began my adventure proper, I already knew this RPG was special.

But this island asylum is big. Really big. It's full of locked doors, hidden rooms, large spaces ripe for some big brawls, a subterranean area waiting to be delved into, oodles of lore—there are hours of rooting around to be done. So I ignored the critical path, had a big old wander, and by the time I finally escaped the island and began my adventure proper, I already knew this RPG was special.

While Tainted Grail is full of bespoke quests sending you off into the open world on countless adventures, these are really just designed to get you out the door so you can stumble upon something cool—a new enemy that will utterly destroy you, a powerful weapon hidden in a crypt, an eccentric immortal being who wants to make a deal. The vibe is very TTRPG, which isn't surprising, given that it's based on one.

And these adventures are actually dangerous. Deadly, even. The villains of Tainted Grail hit hard, and early on you will feel horrifyingly vulnerable. Basic bandits and skeletons can easily spell your doom. And if you stay out at night, you're screwed. Avelon is a miserable, cruel place, cursed and plagued, and you will struggle.

Developer Questline didn't simply up the lethality and call it a day, though. Tainted Grail, unlike The Elder Scrolls, actually has a quality combat system that falls firmly into the skill-based category. It's no Dark Souls, but it's more Dark Souls than Skyrim. So that increased level of challenge feels earned because of the tools you have available to you, and the range of combat styles you can develop.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

With all the options you have at your disposal—which has been further enhanced by DLC additions, letting you, for example, go through this Arthurian fantasy RPG as a kung-fu master—it can be hard to commit to a build. I've been spellblading it up, with my alchemical skills helping to shore up my weaknesses, but every time I encounter a new piece of gear I wonder what else I could create. But you do need to commit eventually. This isn't a game for a jack of all trades.

While Bethesda is more deft at crafting believable, reactive lands, Tainted Grail's world design also deserves its flowers. It's a smaller space, divided into three main areas, and while you can absolutely muck around for hundreds of hours, you can experience most of what it has to offer in 50. But what you'll experience in those 50 hours is so much more meticulously designed, with Questline getting so much out of each location.

It's a game full of aesthetic juxtapositions.

It's a looker, too. What it lacks in fidelity it more than makes up for in the art design department, and it's another place where Dark Souls rears its gorgeously hideous head. Tainted Grail finds beauty in the grim misery of its fantastical post-apocalyptic realm. It's a game full of aesthetic juxtapositions—the arboreal and the horrific, the grounded and alien. Avelon is delightfully strange, and that makes exploration all the more thrilling.

As games grow ever larger and more bloated, my appreciation for richer, better-scoped worlds like Avalon only grows. And this does not indicate a dearth of ambition on Questline's part. Tainted Grail is a complex, elaborate game that will happily devour your days and keep showing you new things.

Clearly people want this—Tainted Grail has done very well for itself, garnering more than 20,000 user reviews on Steam, where its rating sits at Very Positive. It's a reassuring reminder that you do not need a gargantuan studio and big publisher money to make a quality RPG in the Elder Scrolls style.

We don't know how many people are working on Sentinel right now, but we can expect the number to be large. Skyrim had around 100 people working on it, and with Starfield that jumped to more than 400. Tainted Grail was made by 50 people. That's quite the achievement.

So if you're craving a side-quest-heavy sandbox RPG with plenty of sword fights and spellflinging, Tainted Grail should absolutely be your next port of call. And the good news is that there's a demo. No excuses. Go play it.
